# Brief: decide whether we renew the Rotor Club sponsorship

The Rotor Club sponsorship comes up for renewal in October. We have backed them
for six years, the sum has crept from a few hundred pounds to a meaningful line
in the marketing budget, and nobody in the current team can say what we get for
it. I want that settled before the renewal rather than after.

## Background

The arrangement began as a personal connection — a former director's son played
for them — and that connection ended four years ago. What continued is a
standing annual payment, a logo on the shirts, a banner at the ground, and two
tickets to their dinner that somebody from here attends most years.

The club has grown. They are two divisions higher than when we started and the
ground takes about four times the crowd. Their commercial approach has become
correspondingly more professional, which is why the renewal letter this year
proposes an increase and a three-year term.

## What I want to know

- What the sponsorship is actually worth to us, in whatever terms are honest.
  If the honest answer is "goodwill in a town where sixty of our staff live",
  that is a real answer and I will accept it — but it should be said out loud
  rather than assumed, because it implies a different sum and a different set of
  activities than a marketing spend does.
- Whether anybody outside the building associates us with the club at all. A
  short piece of work — ask fifty people in the town centre, ask twenty of our
  own recent applicants — would settle it better than a discussion would.
- What the three-year term commits us to and what our exit looks like if the
  club is relegated, sold, or has the kind of year nobody plans for.
- What else that money would do. Not as a rhetorical device — actually cost two
  alternatives, so the comparison is real.

## What I am not asking for

I am not asking for a recommendation to withdraw. I genuinely do not know what
the right answer is, and a brief that reads as a foregone conclusion will get a
defensive response from the people who value the relationship.

Nor am I asking for a brand study. This is a decision about one line of budget
and it should cost a fraction of what it is deciding.

## Sensitivities

Two of our senior people are personally involved with the club and will hear any
review as a threat to it. Talk to both of them early and directly. If we renew,
they should have been part of the case; if we do not, they should have heard it
from us before they hear it from the club.

The club's own commercial officer is new and keen and will want to meet. Meet
her once you know what we think, not before — a meeting first makes it hard to
say anything other than yes.

## Timing

Six weeks, so there is a fortnight of slack before the October letter. Write it
as two pages: what we get, what it costs, what the alternatives are, and your
view.

## Practicalities

The finance detail you need is in the marketing ledger under a code nobody has
reconciled since 2023, so the first hour of this is going to be establishing
what we have actually paid rather than what we think we have. Do that first —
the sum in everybody's head is four years out of date and low.

There is a file in the shared drive with the original agreement in it. It is
two pages and it says almost nothing, which is itself a finding: whatever we
sign this time should say what happens if either side wants out.

Do not commission a survey firm. Fifty conversations in a town centre, done by
one of us on a Saturday morning, will answer the question well enough and will
cost nothing but the Saturday.
